claim: Loss of neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) is a key pathological event in ALS patients.
source: Loss of neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) is a key pathological event in ALS patients (Fischer et al., 2004; Killian et al., 1994) and in animal models of the disease (Clark et al., 2016; Fischer et al., 2004; Frey et al., 2000; Pun et al., 2006; Tallon et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fischer et al., 2004 and Killian et al., 1994

claim: Loss of neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) is a key pathological event in animal models of ALS.
source: Loss of neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) is a key pathological event in ALS patients (Fischer et al., 2004; Killian et al., 1994) and in animal models of the disease (Clark et al., 2016; Fischer et al., 2004; Frey et al., 2000; Pun et al., 2006; Tallon et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 2016; Fischer et al., 2004; Frey et al., 2000; Pun et al., 2006; Tallon et al., 2016

claim: Denervation of NMJs is observed prior to symptom onset in ALS.
source: Denervation of NMJs is observed prior to symptom onset (Clark et al., 2016; Fischer et al., 2004; Pun et al., 2006; Tallon et al., 2016; Vinsant et al., 2013) and before any significant MN axonal or cell body loss (Fischer et al., 2004; Vinsant et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 2016; Fischer et al., 2004; Pun et al., 2006; Tallon et al., 2016; Vinsant et al., 2013

claim: Denervation of NMJs occurs before any significant motor neuron axonal or cell body loss.
source: Denervation of NMJs is observed prior to symptom onset (Clark et al., 2016; Fischer et al., 2004; Pun et al., 2006; Tallon et al., 2016; Vinsant et al., 2013) and before any significant MN axonal or cell body loss (Fischer et al., 2004; Vinsant et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fischer et al., 2004 and Vinsant et al., 2013

claim: NMJs innervated by fast-fatigable motor neurons are lost early in ALS, followed by fast-fatigue resistant and slow motor neurons.
source: Indeed, NMJs innervated by fast-fatigable MNs are lost early, followed by fast-fatigue resistant and slow MNs (Frey et al., 2000; Pun et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frey et al., 2000 and Pun et al., 2006

claim: The number of motor units declines in parallel with muscle strength in ALS.
source: This is further supported by electromyographic (EMG) recordings showing that the number of MUs declines in parallel with muscle strength (Azzouz et al., 1997; Dantes and McComas, 1991; Hegedus et al., 2007; Hegedus et al., 2008; Kennel et al., 1996; McComas et al., 1971)
evidence: Supported by citations to Azzouz et al., 1997; Dantes and McComas, 1991; Hegedus et al., 2007; Hegedus et al., 2008; Kennel et al., 1996; McComas et al., 1971

claim: Surviving motor units increase in size in animal models and ALS patients.
source: and that surviving MUs increase in size in animal models and in patients (Dantes and McComas, 1991; Dengler et al., 1990; McComas et al., 1971; Schmied et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dantes and McComas, 1991; Dengler et al., 1990; McComas et al., 1971; Schmied et al., 1999

claim: The rescue of neuronal loss in SOD1 mice does not necessarily improve NMJ denervation.
source: However, the rescue of neuronal loss in SOD1 mice does not necessarily improve NMJ denervation (Gould et al., 2006; Parone et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gould et al., 2006; Parone et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2007

claim: Local alterations of synaptic function and molecular signaling take place very early at the NMJ in ALS.
source: In ALS, local alterations of synaptic function and molecular signaling take place very early at the NMJ (Arbour et al., 2015; De Winter et al., 2006; Jokic et al., 2006; Rocha et al., 2013; Taetzsch et al., 2017; Tremblay et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Arbour et al., 2015; De Winter et al., 2006; Jokic et al., 2006; Rocha et al., 2013; Taetzsch et al., 2017; Tremblay et al., 2017

claim: ALS is a non-cell autonomous disease where cell types other than motor neurons contribute to disease pathogenesis.
source: Finally, ALS is a non-cell autonomous disease where cell types other than motor neurons contribute to the disease pathogenesis (Boillée et al., 2006a; Ilieva et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boillée et al., 2006a and Ilieva et al., 2009

claim: SOD1G37R mice are well known for their slow disease progression.
source: SOD1G37R mice (loxSOD1G37R) are well known for their slow disease progression, making it an ideal model to follow single MU changes over time (Boillée et al., 2006b; Lobsiger et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boillée et al., 2006b and Lobsiger et al., 2009

claim: SOD1G37R mice are an ideal model to follow single motor unit changes over time.
source: SOD1G37R mice (loxSOD1G37R) are well known for their slow disease progression, making it an ideal model to follow single MU changes over time (Boillée et al., 2006b; Lobsiger et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by inference from the slow disease progression characteristic and citations to Boillée et al., 2006b and Lobsiger et al., 2009

claim: SOD1G37R mice were crossed to animals expressing a cytoplasmic fluorescent marker (Thy1-YFP line H) in a small random subset of motor neurons.
source: To visualize and follow single MUs in control and ALS mice, we crossed SOD1G37R mice to animals expressing a cytoplasmic fluorescent marker in a small random subset of MNs (Thy1-YFP line H, Figure 1A) (Feng et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2000 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: Repeated in vivo imaging was performed on the Tibialis anterior muscle.
source: Repeated in vivo imaging was performed on the Tibialis anterior muscle since numerous NMJs can be observed near the surface when exposed following a minimally invasive surgery (WT/YFP: N = 5; SOD1G37R/YFP: N = 11).
evidence: Directly stated in the methods description

claim: Numerous NMJs can be observed near the surface of the Tibialis anterior muscle when exposed following a minimally invasive surgery.
source: Repeated in vivo imaging was performed on the Tibialis anterior muscle since numerous NMJs can be observed near the surface when exposed following a minimally invasive surgery (WT/YFP: N = 5; SOD1G37R/YFP: N = 11).
evidence: Stated as rationale for choosing this muscle

claim: Postsynaptic sites were identified in vivo by staining nicotinic receptors with fluorescently labeled α-bungarotoxin.
source: Postsynaptic sites were identified in vivo by staining nicotinic receptors (nAChR) with fluorescently labeled α-bungarotoxin (Li et al., 2011; Turney et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2011 and Turney et al., 2012

claim: All imaging sessions were performed at two-week intervals for up to 5-6 sessions (56-76 days), except for two cases.
source: Except for two cases (animal #23 and #21), all imaging sessions were performed at two--week intervals for up to 5–6 sessions (56–76 days).
evidence: Directly stated in the methods description

claim: The same motor unit arbor was identified on every imaging session through the unique 'pretzel' shape of its NMJs, the branching pattern of the motor axon, and the position of nearby postsynaptic sites.
source: The same MU arbor (axon and its NMJs) was identified on every imaging session through the unique 'pretzel' shape of its NMJs, the branching pattern of the motor axon, and the position of nearby postsynaptic sites (Figure 1A, landmarks, Δ, *, ●).
evidence: Supported by description of methodology and reference to Figure 1A showing landmarks

claim: YFP-labeled axons stayed precisely overlapped with nAChR-rich postsynaptic sites over all imaging sessions in WT/YFP animals (36/36 NMJs, 5/5 MU arbors, N = 5).
source: We followed single MUs in WT/YFP animals and found that YFP-labeled axons stayed precisely overlapped with nAChR-rich postsynaptic sites over all imaging sessions performed (36/36 NMJs, 5/5 MU arbors, N = 5; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data and reference to Figure 1C

claim: Very few changes in axonal branching pattern, postsynaptic nAChRs and presynaptic nerve terminal organization were observed in WT mice.
source: Importantly, very few changes in axonal branching pattern, postsynaptic nAChRs and presynaptic nerve terminal organization were observed.
evidence: Directly stated observation from the imaging data

claim: NMJs of WT mice remained innervated by the same motor unit and were very stable over long periods of time.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Balice-Gordon and Lichtman, 1990; Li et al., 2011; Schaefer et al., 2005; Turney et al., 2012), our results show that NMJs of WT mice remained innervated by the same MU and were very stable over long periods of time.
evidence: Supported by data and citations to Balice-Gordon and Lichtman, 1990; Li et al., 2011; Schaefer et al., 2005; Turney et al., 2012

claim: SOD1G37R/YFP mice were phenotypically and histologically indistinguishable from SOD1G37R mice.
source: Of note, SOD1G37R/YFP mice were phenotypically and histologically indistinguishable from SOD1G37R mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing comparative data

claim: YFP expression did not alter the disease course in SOD1G37R mice.
source: Of note, SOD1G37R/YFP mice were phenotypically and histologically indistinguishable from SOD1G37R mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), showing that YFP expression did not alter the disease course and that YFP-expressing MNs are not more susceptible to the disease.
evidence: Inferred from the indistinguishability of SOD1G37R/YFP and SOD1G37R mice, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: YFP-expressing motor neurons are not more susceptible to ALS disease than non-YFP-expressing motor neurons.
source: Of note, SOD1G37R/YFP mice were phenotypically and histologically indistinguishable from SOD1G37R mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), showing that YFP expression did not alter the disease course and that YFP-expressing MNs are not more susceptible to the disease.
evidence: Inferred from the indistinguishability of SOD1G37R/YFP and SOD1G37R mice, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: YFP-labeled nerve terminals gradually retracted from some nAChR-rich postsynaptic sites in SOD1G37R/YFP mice.
source: We found that YFP-labeled nerve terminals gradually retracted from some nAChR-rich postsynaptic sites (Figure 2A–C, for example, NMJ A1, A3, A4) while other axonal branches remained perfectly overlapped (e.g. NMJ A2).
evidence: Supported by observations shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: Some axonal branches remained perfectly overlapped with postsynaptic sites while others retracted in SOD1G37R/YFP mice.
source: We found that YFP-labeled nerve terminals gradually retracted from some nAChR-rich postsynaptic sites (Figure 2A–C, for example, NMJ A1, A3, A4) while other axonal branches remained perfectly overlapped (e.g. NMJ A2).
evidence: Supported by observations shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: Some NMJs were re-innervated by the motor unit in SOD1G37R/YFP mice.
source: Some NMJs were even re-innervated by the MU (Figure 2A,A4 inset, arrowhead, see below for more details)
evidence: Supported by observations shown in Figure 2A, A4 inset

claim: Most motor units in SOD1 mutant mice (16/19 arbors, 10/11 animals) lost NMJs over several imaging sessions rather than abruptly.
source: Strikingly, most MUs in SOD1 mutant mice (16/19 arbors, 10/11 animals) behaved in a similar fashion, that is, losing NMJs over several imaging sessions rather than abruptly.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from imaging experiments

claim: Partial NMJ losses occurred in 29/253 imaged NMJs across 12/19 arbors in SOD1 mutant mice.
source: These include partial (29/253 imaged NMJs, 12/19 arbors) and complete NMJ losses (38/253 imaged NMJs, 10/19 arbors).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from imaging experiments

claim: Complete NMJ losses occurred in 38/253 imaged NMJs across 10/19 arbors in SOD1 mutant mice.
source: These include partial (29/253 imaged NMJs, 12/19 arbors) and complete NMJ losses (38/253 imaged NMJs, 10/19 arbors).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from imaging experiments

claim: NMJ loss within a single motor unit starts as a slow asynchronous process, occurring independently of axonal degeneration.
source: Thus, NMJ loss within a single MU starts as a slow asynchronous process, occurring independently of axonal degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NMJs are lost over several sessions while other branches remain intact

claim: A number of visualized motor axons and their remaining NMJs were eventually lost in a synchronous manner (7/19 MU arbors, 5/11 mice).
source: A number of visualized motor axons and their remaining NMJs were eventually lost in a synchronous manner (7/19 MU arbors, 5/11 mice; Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data and reference to Figure 3A

claim: Synchronous motor unit degeneration likely reflects an axonal or central event, such as motor neuron death.
source: This phenomenon likely reflects an axonal or central event, such as MN death.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the synchronous loss pattern

claim: Signs of NMJ denervation preceded most synchronous motor unit degenerations (6/7 MU arbors).
source: Importantly, signs of NMJ denervation preceded most of these MU degenerations (Figure 3B, 6/7 MU arbors).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data and reference to Figure 3B

claim: In several cases (11/19 MU arbors), asynchronous NMJ dismantling started more than a month (≥ 3 sessions) prior to global degeneration of the motor unit.
source: In several cases (11/19 MU arbors), asynchronous NMJ dismantling started more than a month (≥ 3 sessions) prior to global degeneration of the MU, again showing that NMJ loss is initially a slow asynchronous process (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data and reference to Figure 3B

claim: Two phases of NMJ loss occur within a motor unit: an initial slow local branch-specific dismantlement, followed by a sudden global axonal degeneration.
source: Hence, we identified two phases of NMJ loss within a MU: an initial slow local branch-specific dismantlement, followed by a sudden global axonal degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal pattern of NMJ losses observed in the imaging data

claim: Nearly all superficial fibers in SOD1G37R/YFP Tibialis anterior were fast-fatigable during the period of imaging (myosin heavy-chain isoforms type IIb or IIx).
source: Indeed, fiber type (indicative of MU type) composition was examined on Tibialis anterior cross sections and revealed that nearly all superficial fibers in SOD1G37R/YFP were fast-fatigable during the period of imaging (myosin heavy-chain isoforms type IIb or IIx; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by fiber type analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Different patterns of motor unit degeneration are unlikely to be due to differences in motor unit types.
source: These different patterns of MU degeneration are unlikely to be due to differences in MU types (Frey et al., 2000; Hegedus et al., 2007; Hegedus et al., 2008; Pun et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from the fiber type composition data showing predominantly fast-fatigable fibers, supported by citations

claim: A vast majority of motor units in SOD1G37R/YFP sprouted toward nearby nAChR-rich postsynaptic sites, forming new synaptic contacts on muscle fibers that they did not innervate initially (76/253 NMJs, 14/19 arbors, 9/11 animals).
source: Surprisingly, a vast majority of MUs in SOD1G37R/YFP also sprouted toward nearby nAChR-rich postsynaptic sites, forming new synaptic contacts on muscle fibers that they did not innervate initially (MU expansions or 'heterologous re-innervation', Figure 4A,B; 76/253 NMJs, 14/19 arbors, 9/11 animals).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data and reference to Figure 4A,B

claim: Motor unit expansions resulted in a net increase in motor unit size which masked the contemporaneous NMJ dismantlement.
source: These numerous expansions resulted in a net increase in MU size which masked the contemporaneous NMJ dismantlement (Figure 4C; 26.0 ± 10.2% loss vs 80.7 ± 32.2% expansions on session 6).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data and reference to Figure 4C

claim: Over half of analyzed motor units both lost and formed new NMJs throughout the imaging process (13/19 arbors, 8/11 animals).
source: Importantly, we found that over half of analyzed MUs both lost and formed new NMJs throughout the imaging process (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, 13/19 arbors, 8/11 animals)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Loss and formation of NMJs can occur simultaneously within a single motor unit.
source: Importantly, we found that over half of analyzed MUs both lost and formed new NMJs throughout the imaging process (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, 13/19 arbors, 8/11 animals), showing that these opposite processes can occur simultaneously within a single MU.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the same motor units showed both losses and gains, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: There is an inverse relationship between the propensity of axonal branches to be lost or to expand.
source: Interestingly, however, there was an inverse relationship between the propensity of axonal branches to be lost or to expand (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: NMJs arising from distal axonal branches were more susceptible to being lost (38 events, n = 253, N = 11, logistic regression, p=0.010).
source: Indeed, NMJs arising from distal axonal branches were more susceptible to being lost (Figure 4D, red dots, 38 events, n = 253, N = 11, logistic regression, p=0.010)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Motor unit expansions were more likely to occur on proximal branches (mainly first-order branches) (76 events, n = 253, N = 11, logistic regression, p=0.001).
source: while MU expansions were more likely to occur on proximal branches (mainly first-order branches) (Figure 4D, blue dots, 76 events, n = 253, N = 11, logistic regression, p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Proximal branches preserve their capacity to re-innervate heterologous NMJs despite the ongoing degeneration of distal branches at the single motor unit level.
source: Hence, proximal branches preserve their capacity to re-innervate heterologous NMJs despite the ongoing degeneration of distal branches at the single MU level.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that proximal branches show more expansions while distal branches show more losses

claim: Few motor units re-innervated their own lost NMJs (autologous re-innervation) (2/21 possibilities).
source: Regardless of this extensive compensation, few MUs re-innervated their own lost NMJs ('autologous re-innervation') and most partial losses were not repaired (Figure 4C, purple; 2/21 and 15/40 possibilities, respectively).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data and reference to Figure 4C

claim: Most partial NMJ losses were not repaired (15/40 possibilities).
source: Regardless of this extensive compensation, few MUs re-innervated their own lost NMJs ('autologous re-innervation') and most partial losses were not repaired (Figure 4C, purple; 2/21 and 15/40 possibilities, respectively).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data and reference to Figure 4C

claim: Some asynchronously lost NMJs had been reinnervated by other motor units.
source: Immunolabeling of all motor axons after the last in vivo session showed that some of these asynchronously lost NMJs had been reinnervated by other MUs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, N = 4)
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Vacated postsynaptic sites were not refractory to reinnervation in general.
source: Immunolabeling of all motor axons after the last in vivo session showed that some of these asynchronously lost NMJs had been reinnervated by other MUs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, N = 4), confirming that these vacated postsynaptic sites were not refractory to reinnervation in general.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that other motor units could reinnervate the lost NMJs, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The initial NMJ pool of surviving motor units gradually receded even though their total size remained stable or increased in most cases due to heterologous expansions.
source: This process led the initial NMJ pool of surviving MUs to gradually recede (Figure 4C, green) even though their total size remained stable or increased in most cases due to heterologous expansions (Figure 4C, blue).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Motor units are highly dynamic during disease progression, with specific branches either expanding or disassembling, rather than being exclusively degenerating or compensating.
source: Altogether, these results show that rather than being exclusively degenerating or compensating, MUs are highly dynamic during disease progression, with specific branches either expanding or disassembling.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that motor units show both losses and gains simultaneously

claim: Asynchronous NMJ dismantling tended to propagate from the first lost NMJ.
source: Interestingly, asynchronous NMJ dismantling tended to propagate from the first lost NMJ (Figure 5A and B; multivariate repeated-measures GLM with logistic distribution, interaction between distance and time: p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of spatial-temporal data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: Adjacent denervation events (<300 μm away) occurred preferentially, but not exclusively, within the next two sessions.
source: Indeed, adjacent events (<300 μm away) occurred preferentially, but not exclusively, within the next two sessions (T2), while remote events (>300 μm) occurred exclusively three or more sessions later (T3+).
evidence: Supported by spatial-temporal analysis of denervation events

claim: Remote denervation events (>300 μm) occurred exclusively three or more sessions after the initial loss.
source: Indeed, adjacent events (<300 μm away) occurred preferentially, but not exclusively, within the next two sessions (T2), while remote events (>300 μm) occurred exclusively three or more sessions later (T3+).
evidence: Supported by spatial-temporal analysis of denervation events

claim: Factors extrinsic to motor axons (i.e. the local neuromuscular environment) interact with the intrinsic properties of motor axons to shape the pattern of NMJ loss in ALS.
source: These results unravel a propagation pattern and suggest that factors extrinsic to motor axons (i.e. the local neuromuscular environment) interact with the intrinsic properties of motor axons (e.g. susceptibility of specific branches), to shape the pattern of NMJ loss in ALS.
evidence: Inferred from the propagation pattern of denervation events

claim: Single motor neurons initially lose NMJs asynchronously while they contemporaneously expand their axonal arbors to form new synaptic contacts in a mouse model of inherited ALS.
source: Our data reveal that single MNs initially lose NMJs asynchronously while they contemporaneously expand their axonal arbors to form new synaptic contacts in a mouse model of inherited ALS (Figure 6).
evidence: Summary of the main findings supported by all the imaging data and Figure 6

claim: The increase in axonal arbor size masks the underlying NMJ dismantlement, effectively reconciling the 'dying-back hypothesis' with the observed motor unit enlargement in animal models and ALS patients.
source: The resulting increase in axonal arbor size masks the underlying NMJ dismantlement, effectively reconciling the 'dying-back hypothesis' with the observed MU enlargement in animal models and ALS patients (Dantes and McComas, 1991; Dengler et al., 1990; Fischer et al., 2004; McComas et al., 1971; Pun et al., 2006; Schaefer et al., 2005).
evidence: Interpretation of findings in context of previous literature, supported by citations

claim: Functional single motor unit recordings from ALS patients identify a majority of enlarged motor units and a subset of abnormally small motor units reflecting extensive NMJ dismantlement.
source: Interestingly, these results are also in line with functional single MU recordings obtained from ALS patients identifying a majority of enlarged MUs and a subset of abnormally small MUs reflecting extensive NMJ dismantlement (Dengler et al., 1990; Schmied et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dengler et al., 1990 and Schmied et al., 1999

claim: NMJ denervation in a motor unit is initially slow and takes place over more than a month in a single motor neuron in SOD1G37R mice.
source: One of our key findings is that NMJ denervation in a MU is initially slow and takes place over more than a month in a single motor neuron in SOD1G37R mice.
evidence: Supported by the longitudinal imaging data showing gradual losses over multiple sessions

claim: There is a long time-window after the onset of NMJ loss during which motor neurons are not globally degenerating and preserve their capacity to reinnervate NMJs.
source: This time course reveals a long time-window after the onset of NMJ loss during which MNs are not globally degenerating and preserve their capacity to reinnervate NMJs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that motor neurons continue to sprout and form new connections while losing others

claim: Peripheral stabilization of NMJs and motor units represents an attractive therapeutic target in the context of ALS.
source: Peripheral stabilization of NMJs and MUs thus represents an attractive therapeutic target in the context of ALS (Cantor et al., 2018; Miyoshi et al., 2017)
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by citations to Cantor et al., 2018 and Miyoshi et al., 2017

claim: The accessibility of the neuromuscular system (i.e. no blood-brain-barrier) makes it particularly attractive for therapeutic intervention.
source: Peripheral stabilization of NMJs and MUs thus represents an attractive therapeutic target in the context of ALS (Cantor et al., 2018; Miyoshi et al., 2017), particularly when considering the accessibility of the neuromuscular system (i.e. no blood-brain-barrier).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the blood-brain barrier

claim: The propagating pattern of events and the asynchronous or multidirectional changes within a single motor unit suggest that neuromuscular factors extrinsic to motor axons affect or contribute to NMJ loss in ALS.
source: The propagating pattern of events and the asynchronous or multidirectional changes within a single MU suggest that neuromuscular factors extrinsic to motor axons (i.e. the local neuromuscular environment) affect or contribute to NMJ loss in ALS.
evidence: Inferred from the spatial-temporal patterns observed in the data

claim: Neuromuscular factors would presumably interact with the intrinsic vulnerability of axonal branches (distal vs proximal, etc.) to shape motor unit dynamism in ALS.
source: These factors would presumably interact with the intrinsic vulnerability of axonal branches (distal vs proximal, etc.) to shape MU dynamism in ALS.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of how extrinsic and intrinsic factors might interact

claim: Chemo-repulsive molecules are mechanisms of therapeutic interest in ALS.
source: Notably, chemo-repulsive molecules (De Winter et al., 2006; Jokic et al., 2006; Maimon et al., 2018; Moloney et al., 2014), availability of trophic factors (Moloney et al., 2014; Taetzsch et al., 2017), enhancement of NMJ stabilizing signals (Miyoshi et al., 2017; Pérez-García and Burden, 2012), secreted pathological proteins or dysfunctional glial cells (Arbour et al., 2015; Arbour et al., 2017) are mechanisms of therapeutic interest.
evidence: Supported by citations to De Winter et al., 2006; Jokic et al., 2006; Maimon et al., 2018; Moloney et al., 2014

claim: Availability of trophic factors is a mechanism of therapeutic interest in ALS.
source: Notably, chemo-repulsive molecules (De Winter et al., 2006; Jokic et al., 2006; Maimon et al., 2018; Moloney et al., 2014), availability of trophic factors (Moloney et al., 2014; Taetzsch et al., 2017), enhancement of NMJ stabilizing signals (Miyoshi et al., 2017; Pérez-García and Burden, 2012), secreted pathological proteins or dysfunctional glial cells (Arbour et al., 2015; Arbour et al., 2017) are mechanisms of therapeutic interest.
evidence: Supported by citations to Moloney et al., 2014 and Taetzsch et al., 2017

claim: Enhancement of NMJ stabilizing signals is a mechanism of therapeutic interest in ALS.
source: Notably, chemo-repulsive molecules (De Winter et al., 2006; Jokic et al., 2006; Maimon et al., 2018; Moloney et al., 2014), availability of trophic factors (Moloney et al., 2014; Taetzsch et al., 2017), enhancement of NMJ stabilizing signals (Miyoshi et al., 2017; Pérez-García and Burden, 2012), secreted pathological proteins or dysfunctional glial cells (Arbour et al., 2015; Arbour et al., 2017) are mechanisms of therapeutic interest.
evidence: Supported by citations to Miyoshi et al., 2017 and Pérez-García and Burden, 2012

claim: Secreted pathological proteins or dysfunctional glial cells are mechanisms of therapeutic interest in ALS.
source: Notably, chemo-repulsive molecules (De Winter et al., 2006; Jokic et al., 2006; Maimon et al., 2018; Moloney et al., 2014), availability of trophic factors (Moloney et al., 2014; Taetzsch et al., 2017), enhancement of NMJ stabilizing signals (Miyoshi et al., 2017; Pérez-García and Burden, 2012), secreted pathological proteins or dysfunctional glial cells (Arbour et al., 2015; Arbour et al., 2017) are mechanisms of therapeutic interest.
evidence: Supported by citations to Arbour et al., 2015 and Arbour et al., 2017

claim: Motor units are not segregated as either degenerating or compensating in ALS.
source: Another main finding is that MUs are not segregated as either degenerating or compensating (Pun et al., 2006; Schaefer et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by the imaging data showing both processes in the same motor units, contrasting with citations to Pun et al., 2006 and Schaefer et al., 2005

claim: The majority of motor units continuously alternate between expansion and disassembly for weeks.
source: Rather, we observed a broad spectrum of MU phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with the majority continuously alternating between expansion and disassembly for weeks.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The asynchronous branch-specific behavior observed in this study contrasts with previous observations made by Schaefer and colleagues using single time point motor unit imaging in the fast-progressing SOD1G93A model.
source: This asynchronous branch-specific behavior contrasts with previous observations made by Schaefer and colleagues using single time point MU imaging in the fast-progressing SOD1G93A model (Schaefer et al., 2005).
evidence: Comparison with previous study, supported by citation to Schaefer et al., 2005

claim: Schaefer and colleagues reported that motor units with fragmented (degenerating) branches lacked thin axons (sprouts) while enlarged motor units lacked signs of degeneration.
source: They reported that MUs with fragmented (degenerating) branches lacked thin axons (sprouts) while enlarged MUs lacked signs of degeneration.
evidence: Summary of findings from Schaefer et al., 2005

claim: Only some motor units underwent gains and losses in the same session.
source: First, our time lapse analysis revealed that only some MUs underwent gains and losses in the same session (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), thus often giving the impression that they are either degenerating or compensating if only a single time point is considered.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The complete dismantlement of a single axonal branch can easily be missed if identified only by the fragmented axonal morphology.
source: Second, we seldom observed a degenerating fragmented branch (9/38, Figures 1 A,2A,A,4 for example), which led us to believe that the complete dismantlement of a single axonal branch can easily be missed if identified only by the fragmented axonal morphology.
evidence: Inferred from the low frequency of observing fragmented branches despite documented losses

claim: The present study only focused on fast-fatigable motor units (MHC IIb and IIx fibers).
source: Another possibility would be that different MU types were considered in these studies, whereas the present study only focused on fast-fatigable MUs (MHC IIb and IIx fibers).
evidence: Stated limitation of the study

claim: Pun et al., 2006 reported no signs of compensatory reinnervation on the surface of the Tibialis anterior.
source: However, Pun et al., 2006 reported no signs of compensatory reinnervation on the surface of the TA (same region as the present study)
evidence: Summary of findings from Pun et al., 2006

claim: Schaefer et al., 2005 imaged a mixture of fast-fatigable and fast-resistant motor units.
source: while Schaefer et al., 2005 imaged a mixture of fast-fatigable and fast-resistant MUs (Sternomastoid, Cleidomastoid and Clavotrapezius), with the former presumably behaving similarly to what we describe here.
evidence: Summary of methods from Schaefer et al., 2005

claim: The pattern of motor unit changes in ALS is reminiscent of post-natal synapse elimination at the NMJ, where the elimination of supernumerary axonal branches is also asynchronous and branch-specific within single motor units.
source: Interestingly, this pattern is reminiscent of post-natal synapse elimination at the NMJ, where the elimination of supernumerary axonal branches is also asynchronous and branch-specific within single MUs (Keller-Peck et al., 2001).
evidence: Comparison with developmental process, supported by citation to Keller-Peck et al., 2001

claim: Similar molecular mechanisms could be involved in ALS motor unit changes and post-natal synapse elimination.
source: This resemblance suggests that similar molecular mechanisms could be involved.
evidence: Speculative inference from the similarity in patterns

claim: Selective axonal branch loss during post-natal synapse elimination was mediated by branch-specific microtubule destabilization.
source: A recent study has shown that selective axonal branch loss during post-natal synapse elimination was mediated by branch-specific microtubule destabilization (Brill et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brill et al., 2016

claim: Pharmacological stabilization of microtubules is beneficial to ALS mice.
source: Interestingly, pharmacological stabilization of microtubules is beneficial to ALS mice (Fanara et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fanara et al., 2007

claim: Microtubule instability could underlie the increased motor unit dynamism in ALS.
source: Interestingly, pharmacological stabilization of microtubules is beneficial to ALS mice (Fanara et al., 2007), suggesting that microtubule instability could underly the increased MU dynamism described here.
evidence: Speculative inference connecting microtubule stabilization benefits with observed motor unit dynamism

claim: Motor neurons failed to re-innervate their lost NMJs, despite preserving their capacity to sprout and form new synaptic contacts onto other heterologous postsynaptic sites.
source: One unexpected finding was that MNs failed to re-innervate their lost NMJs, despite preserving their capacity to sprout and form new synaptic contacts onto other heterologous postsynaptic sites.
evidence: Supported by the imaging data showing low rates of autologous reinnervation but high rates of heterologous reinnervation

claim: Motor axons usually autologously reinnervate their original postsynaptic sites with great fidelity following an axonal lesion.
source: Indeed, motor axons usually autologously reinnervate their original postsynaptic sites with great fidelity following an axonal lesion (Nguyen et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nguyen et al., 2002

claim: Either the heterologous sprout itself or a molecular signal at the endplate may prevent the original axon from reinnervating its target.
source: One possible explanation may be that either the heterologous sprout itself or a molecular signal at the endplate prevents the original axon from reinnervating its target.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the lack of autologous reinnervation

claim: Asynchronous losses occur more frequently on distal branches, which are intrinsically less likely to form sprouts, thus reducing the likelihood of autologous reinnervation occurring.
source: Alternatively, asynchronous losses occur more frequently on distal branches, which seem intrinsically less likely to form sprouts (Figure 4D), thus reducing the likelihood of autologous reinnervation occurring.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing distal branches are more susceptible to loss and less likely to sprout, supported by Figure 4D

claim: NMJs arising from distal branches in complex arbors (higher branch order) are more susceptible than proximal ones at the single motor neuron level in ALS.
source: Consistent with previous results (Tallon et al., 2016), we report that NMJs arising from distal branches in complex arbors (higher branch order) are more susceptible than proximal ones at the single MN level in ALS.
evidence: Supported by the imaging data and citation to Tallon et al., 2016

claim: A larger axonal arborization size increases the energetic load on neurons, thus making them more vulnerable to pathological insults in neurodegenerative disease.
source: These results support the notion that a larger axonal arborization size increases the energetic load on neurons, thus making them more vulnerable to pathological insults in neurodegenerative disease (Le Masson et al., 2014; Pacelli et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Le Masson et al., 2014 and Pacelli et al., 2015

claim: The constant dynamism and the excessive motor unit expansions may further increase the energetic load of motor neurons thus adding to their stress during disease progression.
source: One could speculate that the constant dynamism and the excessive MU expansions further increases the energetic load of MNs thus adding to their stress during disease progression.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the potential consequences of motor unit dynamism

claim: In vivo imaging reveals a previously unsuspected dynamism at the NMJ in an animal model of ALS.
source: Overall, this detailed in vivo analysis reveals a previously unsuspected dynamism at the NMJ in an animal model of ALS.
evidence: Summary statement of the main finding

claim: There is a long temporal window between early branch-specific dismantling and global motor axon degeneration which could be therapeutically exploited in ALS.
source: Our findings highlight a long temporal window between early branch-specific dismantling and global motor axon degeneration which could be therapeutically exploited in ALS (Arbour et al., 2017; Moloney et al., 2014).
evidence: Interpretation of the findings with therapeutic implications, supported by citations to Arbour et al., 2017 and Moloney et al., 2014

claim: Single motor-units are dismantled asynchronously in SOD1G37R mice.
source: Using in vivo imaging of single axons and their NMJs over a three-month period, we identify that single motor-units are dismantled asynchronously in SOD1G37R mice.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the abstract, supported by all imaging data

claim: Weeks prior to complete axonal degeneration, the dismantling of axonal branches is accompanied by contemporaneous new axonal sprouting resulting in synapse formation onto nearby NMJs.
source: We reveal that weeks prior to complete axonal degeneration, the dismantling of axonal branches is accompanied by contemporaneous new axonal sprouting resulting in synapse formation onto nearby NMJs.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the abstract, supported by imaging data showing both losses and gains

claim: Denervation events tend to propagate from the first lost NMJ, consistent with a contribution of neuromuscular factors extrinsic to motor neurons.
source: Denervation events tend to propagate from the first lost NMJ, consistent with a contribution of neuromuscular factors extrinsic to motor neurons, with distal branches being more susceptible.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the abstract, supported by spatial-temporal analysis

claim: Distal branches are more susceptible to denervation than proximal branches.
source: Denervation events tend to propagate from the first lost NMJ, consistent with a contribution of neuromuscular factors extrinsic to motor neurons, with distal branches being more susceptible.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the abstract, supported by branch order analysis

claim: NMJ denervation in ALS is a complex and dynamic process of continuous denervation and new innervation rather than a manifestation of sudden global motor neuron degeneration.
source: These results show that NMJ denervation in ALS is a complex and dynamic process of continuous denervation and new innervation rather than a manifestation of sudden global motor neuron degeneration.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the abstract, supported by all imaging data
